speaker: NARRATOR
text: A small neighborhood in Vietnam: sunshine, kites, street food.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: No deadlines, no rent, no emails.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Truly the best time of anyone's life.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Meet Mui. He is eight years old, and he has just figured out that life is boring.

speaker: MUI
text: Life is boring.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And to be fair, he has evidence.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Every day, Mui wakes up, brushes his teeth, eats breakfast, goes to school, memorizes things,

speaker: NARRATOR
text: comes home, does homework, gets told to do more homework, goes to bed, wakes up, brushes his teeth —

speaker: MUI
text: See?

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And school is the worst part.

speaker: TEACHER
text: Repeat after me.

speaker: THE WHOLE CLASS
text: Repeat after me.

speaker: TEACHER
text: ...Not that part.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Mui feels like a prisoner.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Which, if you have ever been eight years old in a classroom on a hot afternoon, is not a crazy comparison.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Luckily, Mui isn't alone. He has a crew.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Hai. Fast, sneaky, and never, ever sorry.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Tun. Sweet, gentle, and agrees with literally everything.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And Ti. Stylish, confident, and missing her two front teeth.

speaker: TI
text: It'th a look.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Together, they decide that if the adult world is boring, they'll simply change it.

speaker: HAI
text: How?

speaker: MUI
text: Easy. I have three ideas.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Idea number one: who decided a dog has to be called a "dog"? Adults did.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: So the kids make up their own words.

speaker: MUI
text: From now on, a notebook is a "hat".

speaker: HAI
text: A dog is a "banana".

speaker: TUN
text: Okay!

speaker: TI
text: And your feet are your "mouth".

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Brilliant plan. Just one problem: nobody told the adults.

speaker: MOM
text: Mui, go wash your feet before dinner.

speaker: MUI
text: Wash my mouth? With the foot water?

speaker: MOM
text: What?

speaker: MUI
text: Also, the banana ate my hat.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: That went about as well as you'd expect.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Idea number two: if adults get to be in charge, the kids will simply become adults.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Everyone picks a job.

speaker: HAI
text: Chief of police.

speaker: TUN
text: Flight attendant!

speaker: MUI
text: School principal.

speaker: TI
text: Snow White.

speaker: HAI
text: That's not a job.

speaker: TI
text: It is now.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Then they play house, except in their house, the rules are the right way round.

speaker: TI
text: What are you doing?!

speaker: TUN
text: ...My homework?

speaker: MUI
text: In THIS house? Go outside and get dirty, young lady!
tts_text: In this house? Go outside and get dirty, young lady!

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Idea number three, and this is where it gets serious.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The kids hold a court, and the defendants are their own parents.

speaker: HAI
text: Order! Order in the court!

speaker: HAI
text: Charge number one: telling kids that lying is wrong, then telling the neighbor "we're not home" when she comes to borrow money.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: I made that charge up. But if you grew up in Vietnam, you know it's true.

speaker: HAI
text: How do you plead?

speaker: TUN
text: They're at work.

speaker: HAI
text: Then they're guilty. Court dismissed!

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The parents found out,

speaker: NARRATOR
text: and every single kid got a beating.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Here's the thing: it's funny in the book too, until you notice how often it ends this way.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The kids imagine. The adults punish.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The book doesn't lecture you about it.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: It just shows you, again and again, how quickly grown-ups reach for the stick, and lets you sit with that.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: So here's how childhood works.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Renaming everything went badly.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Becoming adults went worse.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And suing your parents went exactly how you'd expect.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Then they tried raising stray dogs as house pets.

speaker: HAI
text: Can we keep them?

speaker: DAD
text: No.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Kids have an idea.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Adults find out.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Everything goes back to normal.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And repeat.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: But here's the twist: the person telling this story isn't eight.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: It's Mui, almost fifty years old, looking back.

speaker: OLD MUI
text: What are you doing?

speaker: HIS KID
text: Texting my girlfriend.

speaker: OLD MUI
text: At your age?

speaker: OLD MUI
text: ...Actually, at your age I was suing my dad.
tts_text: Actually, at your age I was suing my dad.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Little Mui thought adults were boring, and Old Mui has become one.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: So who is this book really for?

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The book says it's for anyone who was once a child, which is everyone.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Its last chapter is about a train with no ticket inspector.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: You can go back to childhood any time you like. Nobody checks.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: So, is it worth the ticket?

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The good stuff first: it's short, and it's funny.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And it's told in a child's voice, which turns out to be the sharpest weapon against adult nonsense ever invented.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: It won the S.E.A. Write Award in 2010 and sold hundreds of thousands of copies in Vietnam.
tts_text: It won the Sea Write Award in twenty ten, and sold hundreds of thousands of copies in Vietnam.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Mostly, I assume, to adults who felt personally attacked.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: Now, to be fair, if you want a big plot, this isn't it.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: The book is a string of episodes, not one big adventure.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And if you read the English version, some reviewers say a bit of the Southern Vietnamese flavor gets lost on the way.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: So who should read it? Anyone who was once eight,

speaker: NARRATOR
text: and especially anyone who now has an eight-year-old.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: And so, Mui and his friends grew up, became sensible adults, and never did anything silly ever again.

speaker: OLD MUI
text: ...Banana.

speaker: NARRATOR
text: For about forty years.
